title: Is probate still mandatory for a will in India after Section 213 was repealed?
seo_title: Is Probate Still Mandatory After Section 213 Repeal?
meta_description: Section 213 of the Succession Act was omitted in December 2025, ending mandatory probate for some wills. Who was covered, and why probate still helps.
format: case-law explainer built on one real judgment
intro: For decades, a Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jain testator whose will fell within the old presidency-town jurisdictions of Calcutta, Madras or Bombay, or whose will concerned immovable property in those areas, could not act on that will without first obtaining probate. The Repealing and Amending Act, 2025 omitted the provision that created that requirement, Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, with effect from 20 December 2025. As on this date, probate of such a will is no longer compulsory, though it remains available and is often still worth getting.

This is a genuine change, not a restatement of an old position, and it lands directly on top of advice that firms and individuals have been giving in Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai for generations. Anyone who was told a few years ago that a Kolkata-made Hindu will absolutely needed probate before it could be acted on should treat that advice as needing a fresh look, while understanding that the underlying reasons probate was useful have not disappeared just because the mandate has.

sections.heading: What Section 213 actually required, and who it covered
paragraphs: Section 213, before its omission, barred an executor or legatee from establishing a right under a will in any court unless probate of the will, or letters of administration with the will annexed, had been obtained. Read with Section 57, the requirement was never a general rule for every will in India. It applied to wills made by Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs and Jains falling within clauses (a) and (b) of Section 57, which covered wills made within the former presidency towns of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay, and wills made anywhere else concerning immovable property situated within those towns.

A Hindu will made in, say, Noida, concerning property only in Uttar Pradesh, was never caught by Section 213 in the first place, because it fell outside the geographic reach of clauses (a) and (b). This is a point the Allahabad High Court has reaffirmed, including in a ruling reported in November 2025 holding that probate is not required for a Hindu will made outside those specified territories, or concerning immovable property outside them, following the reasoning the Supreme Court set out in Clarence Pais. The practical significance of the 2025 repeal is greatest for wills that do fall inside the old presidency-town categories, which until the repeal had no way around the mandatory requirement.

sections.heading: What the Repealing and Amending Act, 2025 changed
paragraphs: The Repealing and Amending Act, 2025 omitted Section 213, along with consequential changes to cross-references in Sections 3 and 370 of the Succession Act, with effect from 20 December 2025. Multiple independent commentaries describe this as removing a colonial-era, territory-based mandate that had long been criticised as arbitrary, since it turned on where the testator or the property happened to sit rather than on any feature of the will itself.

What the repeal did not do is abolish probate as a legal tool, and it did not touch the parts of the Succession Act that make probate conclusive evidence of a will's validity once granted, or that let a court test a disputed will through a probate proceeding. It also does not disturb probate proceedings that were already underway, or grants already made, before the repeal took effect. A family mid-way through a contested probate petition in the Calcutta High Court's testamentary jurisdiction when the repeal came into force continues under the old framework for that proceeding.

sections.heading: Why probate can still be the sensible route even though it is not compulsory
paragraphs: Removing the mandate changes what the law requires before an executor can act, not what banks, registrars and buyers will accept without question. A bank releasing a large fixed deposit, a sub-registrar mutating a flat, or a buyer paying for inherited property still routinely ask for probate or at least a succession certificate before they will deal with an executor or heir, because probate gives them a court-tested document that protects them from a later claim by someone else. None of that institutional caution disappears just because Section 213 no longer forces the executor's hand.

Probate also remains the strongest answer to a disputed will. If a sibling is likely to challenge the will's validity, genuineness or the testator's mental capacity, going through a probate proceeding settles that question with a court order that is difficult to reopen later, whereas simply acting on an unprobated will leaves the door open to a suit years afterward. Families with significant or contested estates, in Kolkata or anywhere else, generally gain more from voluntary probate than they lose by not being compelled into it.

sections.heading: Who should rethink, and who should not
paragraphs: An executor with a straightforward, uncontested Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jain will that falls inside the old Calcutta, Madras or Bombay categories, where every beneficiary agrees and the estate is modest, may now be able to act on the will and transfer assets without probate, subject to what individual institutions choose to accept. That is a real simplification for small, cooperative estates that previously had to go through a court process purely because of where the testator lived.

An executor dealing with a larger estate, disputed shares, immovable property with an uncertain title history, or beneficiaries who do not get along should not read the repeal as removing the reasons probate existed. The repeal removes a compulsion; it does not remove the practical value of a court-tested grant in exactly the situations where disputes are most likely. Wills made by Indian Christians raise a separate wrinkle, since at least one published analysis reads the old Section 213 as also reaching their wills in some circumstances, a point on which commentators do not fully agree, so that community's position should be checked specifically rather than assumed from the Hindu-will analysis.

Executors who acted, or are currently acting, on the assumption that probate was compulsory should not assume the opposite now either. The safer habit, for the next few years at least, is to ask the specific institution involved, bank, registrar, insurer or buyer, what it will accept, rather than assuming the repeal has already changed every counter's practice. Internal policies at banks and registration offices tend to lag a change like this by some months, and an executor who shows up without probate on the strength of a December 2025 law change may still be asked to get one anyway until that catches up.

sections.heading: What this means specifically for Kolkata estates
paragraphs: Kolkata families feel this change more than most, since the former presidency town of Calcutta is one of the three territories Section 213 named, and the Calcutta High Court's testamentary jurisdiction has handled a steady stream of probate petitions over the decades precisely because of that geographic trigger. An executor dealing with a Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or Jain testator's estate confined to Kolkata, with cooperative heirs and no immovable property dispute, is exactly the profile that benefits most from the repeal, since the compulsion that previously sent even simple, agreed estates into the testamentary court no longer applies to them.

That said, Kolkata's banks, the Kolkata Municipal Corporation's mutation desk and West Bengal's land registration offices built their own internal practice around decades of mandatory probate, and none of that practice changes automatically on the date a central statute is amended. An executor should expect to explain the 2025 repeal to a counter clerk who may not yet be aware of it, and carrying a copy of the amending Act or a reasoned summary of the change, rather than assuming the point will be taken on trust, saves a repeat visit.

faqs.q: Do I still need probate for a Hindu will made in Kolkata after the 2025 change?
faqs.a: It is no longer compulsory as a matter of law, since the Repealing and Amending Act, 2025 omitted Section 213 with effect from 20 December 2025. Banks, registrars and buyers may still ask for probate or a succession certificate before dealing with an executor, so in practice it often remains the smoother route.

faqs.q: Was probate ever required for a Hindu will made outside Bengal, Madras or Bombay?
faqs.a: No. Section 213, before its repeal, only applied to wills falling within clauses (a) and (b) of Section 57, which covered the former presidency towns and property located there. Courts, including the Allahabad High Court, have repeatedly held that a Hindu will made elsewhere, concerning property elsewhere, never attracted the mandatory requirement.

faqs.q: Does the repeal of Section 213 affect a probate case that is already pending in court?
faqs.a: No. Commentary on the 2025 repeal is consistent that pending probate proceedings and grants already made are unaffected. The change governs whether probate is compulsory going forward, not what happens to matters already before the court.

faqs.q: If probate is no longer mandatory, should I skip it to save time and cost?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Probate gives banks, registrars and buyers a court-tested document and makes it far harder for a disgruntled heir to reopen the will's validity later. For a modest, uncontested estate it may now be skippable; for a large or disputed one, voluntary probate usually still protects the executor better than acting without it.

references: Indian Succession Act, 1925, Section 213 (omitted), read with Section 57
Repealing and Amending Act, 2025, effective 20 December 2025
Clarence Pais v Union of India (Supreme Court), as applied by the Allahabad High Court in its November 2025 ruling on probate for Hindu wills outside the specified territories
verification_notes: AUDIENCE: HNI/domestic (Kolkata and other presidency-town families), relevant to NRI heirs of such estates too. TARGET QUERY: is probate still mandatory for a will in India after Section 213 was repealed. DEMAND EVIDENCE: a recent, specifically dated legal development (repeal effective 20 December 2025) that several independent law-related publications wrote about within the last year, which is itself the demand signal relied on here; no search-volume tool was used, so no figure is stated. Omission of Section 213 by the Repealing and Amending Act, 2025, effective 20 December 2025: confirmed from at least two independent sources (Lexology/CMS-IndusLaw and ThePrint), both giving the same effective date; SCC Online Blog and Bar and Bench corroborate the same point, giving four sources in total. Scope of the old Section 213 (Hindu/Buddhist/Sikh/Jain wills within Section 57(a)/(b) presidency-town categories): confirmed from two sources (Lexology/CMS-IndusLaw and the Allahabad High Court ruling as reported by LiveLaw), which both tied the requirement to Section 57(a) and (b). The November 2025 Allahabad High Court ruling citing Clarence Pais: reported by LiveLaw; a second, older Allahabad ruling applying the same reasoning (Ashok Kumar Dhawan) was found in search results and used only to corroborate the general proposition, not as a second citation of the 2025 ruling itself, since I did not open the certified judgment text for either case; the case names and the Clarence Pais reference are stated as reported by these sources, not verified against the full judgment. Existing probate proceedings and grants being unaffected by the repeal: stated by at least two independent commentaries (Lexology/CMS-IndusLaw and Bar and Bench) in materially the same terms. The disputed point about Section 213 also reaching Indian Christian wills: reported by only one source (SCC Online Blog) as a minority or disputed reading, and is flagged in the text as unsettled rather than stated as fact, consistent with the STRICT_VERIFICATION instruction to state only what sources agree on.
